Algebraic Dead Directions in LayerNorm Transformers: A Forward-Pass-Only Diagnostic at LLM Scale

Tejas Pradeep Shirodkar Affiliation: IIIT, Hyderabad Email: tejas.shirodkar@research.iiit.ac.in    P. J. Narayanan Affiliation: IIIT, Hyderabad Email: pjn@iiit.ac.in
Abstract

Pretrained transformers sit near singular minima of the loss, where the Fisher information metric degenerates along dead directions: directions in parameter space along which the directional Fisher vanishes. Locating such a direction normally needs a forward pass and an eigendecomposition of activations, or a sampling-based complexity estimate; none returns a direction computable from the network’s parameters alone. We give one, for LayerNorm transformers. The inverse-scale direction γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| of the LayerNorm affine is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance, for any input distribution, and induces a corresponding dead direction in parameter space. It is read from the LN scale parameter alone, with no forward or backward pass and no eigensolve: the cheapest dead-direction read, specific to LayerNorm. We test it on 1414 pretrained transformers (99 LayerNorm, 55 RMSNorm; 160160M-3535B; language and vision objectives). At random initialisation the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction (one forward pass, direct SVD) to four decimal places on 9/99/9 LayerNorm models, and is correctly absent on 5/55/5 RMSNorm models, which lack the mean-subtraction projector that creates it. On the trained checkpoint the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ∼103×{\sim}10^{3}\times and further dead directions open; the random-init-to-trained gap is a one-forward-pass, per-checkpoint readout of singular structure along the predicted coordinate. Two consequences follow in closed form: the residual stream’s smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on 13/1413/14 transformers measured on their own input distribution, the one exception (Gemma 44-3131B) a genuine dead direction the same read pinpoints; and the kernel direction’s presence classifies a transformer’s normalisation from the parameters alone.

1 Introduction

Trained transformers do not sit at isolated minima of their loss. The parameter spaces of overparameterised models contain analytic singular sets along which the Fisher information metric degenerates (Watanabe, 2009), and a trained network sits at one specific configuration on that singular structure. The practical question is which configuration: along which directions in parameter space is the loss flat, and what does that flatness look like at the network’s actual weights? An answer in original parameter coordinates would let practitioners identify dead subspaces without sampling, gradient access, or the 10410^{4}–10610^{6} forward–backward passes per checkpoint that the local learning coefficient (Lau et al., 2025; Hoogland et al., 2024, LLC;) requires. The dead-direction framework of Shirodkar (2026) gives such an answer in original parameter coordinates, deriving a network’s flat directions (dead directions) from a KFAC factorisation of its Fisher. This paper develops its LayerNorm case, where the answer is closed-form: a single dead direction read from one parameter with no forward pass, validated across pretrained transformers at LLM scale.

Singular learning theory locates these dead directions through Hironaka resolution (Watanabe, 2009), a coordinate change that recasts the KL divergence in normal-crossing form so the local real log canonical threshold is readable. Information geometry encodes the same structure as a degeneration of the Fisher metric (Amari et al., 2006; Amari, 2016), but presupposes the metric is non-singular and so is silent on the singular set itself. Recent activation-spectrum work tracks σmin\sigma_{\min} (Jha and Reagen, 2026; Ettori et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), weight-update SVD (Xu, 2026), and Marchenko–Pastur deviations on pretrained weights (Staats et al., 2024), and the rank-collapse line (Dong et al., 2021; Noci et al., 2022) characterises the same observable in pure-attention chains. None of these methods returns a specific direction in a specific architecture that is computable from the network’s affine parameters alone. We give one, the framework’s LayerNorm instance: a closed-form unit vector in residual-stream space, read from the LayerNorm scale parameter alone, that lies in the kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance for any input distribution. The KFAC factorisation of Martens and Grosse (2015) is the measurement primitive that makes this direction parameter-readable rather than only forward-pass-readable.

Our central architecture-side prediction admits a four-decimal test on real LLMs. Write γ∈ℝd\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for the LayerNorm scale parameter and let u⊥u_{\bot} denote the bottom singular direction of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance. For any LayerNorm-equipped transformer, this covariance is rank-deficient exactly along the inverse-scale direction v∗:=γ−1/‖γ−1‖v^{*}:=\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|, a unit vector readable from the LN affine parameter alone with no forward pass required (Proposition 2, §3). For RMSNorm, lacking the mean-subtraction projector, no such universal direction exists (Proposition 3). Both predictions are theorems of the theory paper, restated with proof sketches in §3 and subjected here to a four-decimal test at LLM scale. The two propositions partition any pretrained transformer into two classes: LN models should exhibit the predicted direction algebraically; RMSNorm models should not. We test both at random initialisation and on the trained checkpoint, and treat the gap between the two as a third measurement.

The match is sharp on every applicable model. On 99 LN-equipped pretrained transformers spanning next-token CE, supervised image classification, DINO-SSL, MAE-reconstruction, contrastive-image-text, and predictive-video-SSL objectives, the cosine alignment satisfies |cos⁡(u⊥,v∗)|≥0.9999|\cos(u_{\bot},v^{*})|\geq 0.9999 at random initialisation (mean 0.999990.99999); the 55 RMSNorm models sit at the random-direction null. To track how training deepens the kernel beyond this algebraic baseline, we use the per-block Schur ratio R⁡(h):=λmin​(Aℓ)/(Aℓ)u,uR(h):=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})/(A_{\ell})_{u,u} comparing the smallest activation-covariance eigenvalue at block ℓ\ell against the eigenvalue along the predicted direction u=γ−1/‖γ−1‖u=\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|; its complement Δγ:=1−R⁡(h)∈[0,1]\Delta_{\gamma}:=1-R(h)\in[0,1] measures how much deeper than uu the actual bottom of the spectrum sits. Δγ≈0\Delta_{\gamma}\approx 0 means the predicted direction is the bottom; Δγ≈1\Delta_{\gamma}\approx 1 means the bottom is orders of magnitude smaller along some other direction. On the Pythia LN sweep, random-init Δγ\Delta_{\gamma} reads ≈0.37\approx 0.37 at h=512h{=}512 (finite-NN Marchenko–Pastur drift ∼2​h/N−h/N\sim 2\sqrt{h/N}-h/N, largest at the smallest cell) and within ±0.06\pm 0.06 of zero at h≥768h\geq 768; the trained checkpoint saturates at ≈1\approx 1 across all sizes, a ∼103×\sim\!10^{3}\times deepening along the same coordinate. The gap between random-init and trained Δγ\Delta_{\gamma} is the diagnostic: training opens dead directions strictly deeper than the architectural baseline establishes.

Contributions.
  1. 1.

    Algebraic baseline + gap diagnostic on 1414 pretrained transformers. The predicted dead direction γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| matches the measured bottom singular direction to four decimal places on 9/99/9 LN models at random init (centered protocol; mean |cos|>0.99999|\cos|>0.99999), and is correctly absent on 5/55/5 RMSNorm models (|cos|≤0.10|\cos|\leq 0.10 centered). On the same Pythia size sweep, the Schur ratio collapses from random-init Δγ≈0.37\Delta_{\gamma}\approx 0.37 at h=512h{=}512 (within ±0.06\pm 0.06 of zero at h≥768h\geq 768) to Δγ≈1\Delta_{\gamma}\approx 1 trained across all sizes, with a 33–18×18\times directional beat over the axis-aligned default (§4, Tab. 1).

  2. 2.

    σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance on 13/1413/14 pretrained transformers. A closed-form corollary of the LN-kernel analysis predicts the residual stream’s smallest singular value cannot fall below its input-embedding value at any block, σmin​(Xℓ)/σmin​(X0)≥1\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})/\sigma_{\min}(X_{0})\geq 1, read from a single forward pass with no gradient access. The bound holds on 1313 of 1414 pretrained transformers once each model is read on its own input distribution. The one exception, Gemma4-31B, is itself a detection win: the same read pinpoints a genuine intrinsic dead direction in its residual stream, above the fp3232 measurement floor, at the depth where the corollary’s no-cancellation hypothesis fails (§4, Fig. 3; App. A.6).

  3. 3.

    LN/RMSNorm algebraic dichotomy as a normalisation-architecture classifier. The same closed-form test partitions any pretrained transformer’s normalisation choice: LN-equipped models exhibit the γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| kernel direction; RMSNorm models do not (no γ\gamma-derived universal kernel). The dichotomy generalises to alternative norms by structural inspection (InstanceNorm, DyT, ScaleNorm, FixUp, WeightNorm classify by the same projector test; BatchNorm and GroupNorm are structurally different and remain open empirical cells; App. A.5).

2 Background and notation

For an analytic statistical family {pθ}\{p_{\theta}\} with Fisher information F⁡(θ)F(\theta) and pθ0=p∗p_{\theta_{0}}=p^{*}, the singular set Σ={θ:detF⁡(θ)=0}\Sigma=\{\theta:\det F(\theta)=0\} is where FF loses rank. Singular learning theory (Watanabe, 2009) shows minima of K(θ):=KL(p∗∥pθ)K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(p^{*}\|p_{\theta}) in singular models lie on Σ\Sigma, and that KK vanishes along a unit direction uu at θ0\theta_{0} at a rate controlled by an integer KL order k≥1k\geq 1: K⁡(θ0+t​u)=c​t2​k+O⁡(t2​k+1)K(\theta_{0}+tu)=c\,t^{2k}+O(t^{2k+1}). In the resolved local normal form K∼u2​k+v12+⋯+vm2K\sim u^{2k}+v_{1}^{2}+\cdots+v_{m}^{2}, the local RLCT is λ=1/(2​k)+m/2\lambda=1/(2k)+m/2 (Hironaka, 1964; Watanabe, 2009); the directional invariant our rate theorem returns is the 1/(2​k)1/(2k) contribution.

For a layer with weights WℓW_{\ell}, the KFAC factorisation (Martens and Grosse, 2015) gives Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell} with Aℓ:=𝔼⁡[Xℓ−1​Xℓ−1⊤]A_{\ell}:=\mathbb{E}[X_{\ell-1}X_{\ell-1}^{\top}] and Gℓ:=𝔼⁡[δℓ​δℓ⊤]G_{\ell}:=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}^{\top}]; thus λmin​(Fℓ)=λmin​(Aℓ)​λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(F_{\ell})=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})\,\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}). We use Aℓ,GℓA_{\ell},G_{\ell} as canonical names. Other recurring symbols: LL depth, ℓ\ell layer index, hh hidden width; Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} activation matrix; uu dead direction (Def. 1); Kfwd​(ℓ)K^{\mathrm{fwd}}(\ell) forward shortest-weighted-path distance on a residual DAG.

2.1 Related work

SLT-side invariants and spectral monitoring.

Singular learning theory (Watanabe, 2009; Watanabe, 2018) locates the complexity of an overparameterised model in the local geometry of its loss-singular set; the local learning coefficient (Lau et al., 2025; Hoogland et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Plummer, 2025, LLC;) estimates Watanabe’s RLCT via SGLD sampling and provides the established Bayesian-posterior reading of singular complexity. The diagnostic this paper advances reads the same singular structure off a network’s affine parameters in closed form, without sampling, and is therefore complementary to LLC’s integrated Bayesian quantity. A parallel spectral-monitoring lineage tracks activation or weight spectra as generalisation-correlated signatures (Jha and Reagen, 2026; Ettori et al., 2025; Xu, 2026; Khanh et al., 2026; Staats et al., 2024; Boix-Adsera et al., 2023); we sit at the bottom of the activation spectrum specifically, with an algebraic prediction for which direction u⊥u_{\bot} is at any LN-equipped pretrained transformer. Random-matrix characterisations of the Fisher / Hessian spectrum at large width (Pennington and Worah, 2018; Karakida et al., 2019; Karakida et al., 2021) are used only defensively in the n/dn/d calibration of the measurement protocol. Top-of-spectrum sharpness work (Hessian-eigenvalue tracking via Lanczos/Hutchinson (Sagun et al., 2018; Ghorbani et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2020), edge of stability (Cohen et al., 2021)) and circuit-level mech-interp phase detection (Olsson et al., 2022; Nanda et al., 2023) are complementary axes that probe different objects.

Residual-stream + LayerNorm geometry.

Papyan et al. (2020) characterised neural collapse at the terminal phase of training. Dong et al. (2021) show pure-attention chains lose rank doubly-exponentially with depth; Noci et al. (2022) characterise the signal-propagation mechanism. Corollary 4 below is the opposite conclusion in the residual case: identity skips turn the same σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) observable from a collapse into a rate-00 preservation along the residual stream. Concurrent dimensional-collapse work (Wang et al., 2025) reports residual-stream activations resist rank collapse compared to attention outputs in pretrained transformers; we sharpen this to a σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance prediction with an analytic mechanism and per-architecture falsifications (§4). PCA-based activation rotation (Ashkboos et al., 2024) folds the LN mean-subtraction projector M=I−(1/d)​𝟏𝟏⊤M=I-(1/d)\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} into adjacent weights as a compression rewrite, the γ≡1\gamma\equiv 1 case of our kernel-direction identity. We generalise to the γ\gamma-weighted direction γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| (Proposition 2), which is what the bottom singular direction of the post-final-norm centred covariance actually tracks on trained models with γ\gamma-dispersion (DINOv2-base, DINOv3-ViT-L). SliceGPT’s RMSNorm rotational equivariance (exploited there for compression) is the same property our Proposition 3 reads as a structural classifier: rotational equivariance means no preferred direction is dead a priori. We use this dichotomy as a diagnostic, identified algebraically in the LN case and structurally in the residual-DAG case (Corollary 4), with no weight modification. Riechers (2024) characterises the geometry and dynamics of LayerNorm as a forward-map operator; the forward-pass-free γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| kernel-direction identity (Proposition 2) and the corresponding negative differential for RMSNorm (Proposition 3) complement that forward-map analysis with a kernel-direction identity readable from the affine alone.

Empirical Fisher and KFAC.

Kunstner et al. (2019) cautioned about the empirical Fisher; our measurement protocol uses an expected-Fisher KFAC approximation (Martens and Grosse, 2015; Grosse and Martens, 2016), with Eschenhagen et al. (2023) as the transformer-generalisation reference and EKFAC (George et al., 2018) as the eigenbasis variant. We use the KFAC factorisation here as a measurement primitive only; the analytical use of KFAC for deriving per-layer singular collapse rates is established in Shirodkar, 2026.

3 The LN-kernel direction

Pretrained transformers carry a closed-form dead direction that a practitioner can read off a single architectural parameter. The four results we state below stake out this claim. Two are algebraic identities of the LayerNorm and RMSNorm forward maps; the third lifts those identities to a depth-invariance statement about residual-stream activations; the fourth turns the algebraic kernel direction into a quantitative per-checkpoint diagnostic. Full proofs are in the theory paper, where these are Proposition 63 (the LayerNorm and RMSNorm kernels), Corollary 58 (σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance), and Lemma 18 (the Schur ratio).

Definition 1 (Dead direction).

A unit direction u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a dead direction at θ0\theta_{0} if u⊤​F​(θ⁡(t))​u→0u^{\top}F(\theta(t))u\to 0 as t→0t\to 0 along θ⁡(t):=θ0+t​u\theta(t):=\theta_{0}+tu. The KL order along uu is the integer k≥1k\geq 1 with K⁡(θ⁡(t))=c​t2​k+O⁡(t2​k+1)K(\theta(t))=c\,t^{2k}+O(t^{2k+1}), c>0c>0. (Unrelated to the activation-level “dead ReLU” phenomenon despite the lexical overlap.)

The starting observation is that LayerNorm’s mean-subtraction projector forces a deterministic kernel direction at the output of every LN block, for any input distribution. The direction is the inverse of the LN scale parameter, normalised. This is a property of LN’s forward map alone: any LN-equipped network carries it the moment its weights are initialised, before any training has occurred.

Proposition 2 (LayerNorm kernel direction).

Let LN⁡(x)=γ⊙P​x‖P​x‖/d+β\mathrm{LN}(x)=\gamma\odot\frac{Px}{\|Px\|/\sqrt{d}}+\beta with mean-subtraction projector P=I−(1/d)​𝟏d​𝟏d⊤P=I-(1/d)\mathbf{1}_{d}\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}, and let X∈ℝdX\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be any random input with P​X≠0PX\neq 0 almost surely. Write C:=Cov⁡(LN⁡(X))C:=\cov(\mathrm{LN}(X)). If every γi≠0\gamma_{i}\neq 0, then C⋅γ−1=0C\cdot\gamma^{-1}=0 where γ−1:=(γ1−1,…,γd−1)⊤\gamma^{-1}:=(\gamma_{1}^{-1},\ldots,\gamma_{d}^{-1})^{\top}, with unit kernel direction v∗=γ−1/‖γ−1‖.v^{*}=\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|. The direction is readable from the LN affine alone, with no forward pass. (If γ\gamma has zero coordinates Z={i:γi=0}Z=\{i:\gamma_{i}=0\}, C⋅ei=0C\cdot e_{i}=0 for every i∈Zi\in Z.)

Sketch.

The mean-subtraction projector annihilates 𝟏d\mathbf{1}_{d} (𝟏d⊤​P=0\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}P=0), so 𝟏d⊤​x~LN​(X)=0\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{LN}}(X)=0 almost surely and Cov⁡(x~LN)​𝟏d=0\cov(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{LN}})\mathbf{1}_{d}=0. With LN⁡(X)=diag⁡(γ)​x~LN​(X)+β\mathrm{LN}(X)=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{LN}}(X)+\beta, C=diag⁡(γ)​Cov⁡(x~LN)​diag​(γ)C=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma)\cov(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{LN}})\mathrm{diag}(\gamma). Since diag⁡(γ)​γ−1=𝟏d\mathrm{diag}(\gamma)\gamma^{-1}=\mathbf{1}_{d} coordinate-wise, C​γ−1=diag⁡(γ)​Cov⁡(x~LN)​𝟏d=0C\gamma^{-1}=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma)\cov(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{LN}})\mathbf{1}_{d}=0. ∎

The proof is short because LayerNorm does the work: the projector PP algebraically kills 𝟏d\mathbf{1}_{d}, and the subsequent γ\gamma-rescaling carries that kernel to γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|. The contribution is not the algebra but the empirical claim it forces. Any pretrained LN-equipped transformer should exhibit a bottom singular direction that aligns with γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| at random initialisation; deviation falsifies the prediction.

The complementary case is RMSNorm. Lacking a mean-subtraction projector, RMSNorm has no operator that annihilates a fixed direction independent of input. Every γi≠0\gamma_{i}\neq 0 leaves the RMSNorm output covariance full rank for any non-degenerate input distribution. We state this as a negative differential to make the dichotomy formal.

Proposition 3 (RMSNorm has no universal kernel).

For an RMSNorm operator RMSNorm⁡(x)=γ⊙x/‖x‖2/d\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x)=\gamma\odot x/\sqrt{\|x\|^{2}/d} with every γi≠0\gamma_{i}\neq 0, no unit direction v⁡(γ)v(\gamma) depending only on γ\gamma universally satisfies v⊤​Cov⁡(RMSNorm⁡(X))​v=0v^{\top}\cov(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(X))v=0 across all input distributions XX with Cov⁡(X)≻0\cov(X)\succ 0.

Sketch.

RMSNorm⁡(X)=r⁡(X)⋅γ⊙X\mathrm{RMSNorm}(X)=r(X)\cdot\gamma\odot X with r⁡(X)>0r(X)>0 a positive scalar; RMSNorm\mathrm{RMSNorm} has no projector that annihilates a fixed direction independent of XX. For X∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), r⁡(X)​X=d⋅X/‖X‖r(X)X=\sqrt{d}\cdot X/\|X\| is uniform on Sd−1S^{d-1} scaled by d\sqrt{d}, so Cov⁡(r⁡(X)​X)=Id\cov(r(X)X)=I_{d}. Hence Cov⁡(RMSNorm⁡(X))=diag​(γ)2≻0\cov(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(X))=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma)^{2}\succ 0, with no zero direction. A universal kernel direction v⁡(γ)v(\gamma) would require a zero direction for every input distribution; this counter-example rules it out. ∎

Together the two propositions stake an architectural dichotomy: a single closed-form test on the affine parameter classifies any pretrained transformer’s normalisation choice, before any forward pass. LN-equipped models exhibit the predicted direction; RMSNorm models do not.

The next result lifts the LN-kernel observation to a depth-invariance claim that holds under either normalisation. Residual streams in modern transformers compose blocks via additive-identity skips, Xℓ+1=Xℓ+F⁡(Xℓ)X_{\ell+1}=X_{\ell}+F(X_{\ell}). The skip provides a zero-cost backward path for the bottom singular direction, so the smallest singular value cannot decrease block-to-block under a non-cancellation hypothesis on the residual branch. This is independent of whether the block uses LN or RMSNorm.

Corollary 4 (Residual-stream σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance).

On a residual DAG with exact-identity skips, the smallest singular value of the residual-stream activation matrix satisfies σmin​(Xℓ)/σmin​(X0)≥1\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})/\sigma_{\min}(X_{0})\geq 1 at every block under canonical alignment of dead directions and the no-cancellation hypothesis at the bottom-of-active-spectrum direction. (The hypothesis is not generic on trained networks; we report it as a checkpoint-failable architectural property.)

Sketch.

Path decomposition: Xℓ=X0+∑p∈𝒫⁡(ℓ)δpX_{\ell}=X_{0}+\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}(\ell)}\delta_{p} where 𝒫⁡(ℓ)\mathcal{P}(\ell) enumerates non-skip paths reaching block ℓ\ell. Under no-cancellation at the bottom-of-active-spectrum direction, the perturbations δp\delta_{p} do not destructively interfere with X0X_{0} along that direction, so the sum’s bottom singular value is bounded below by the input’s. Cancellation breaks the bound; we observe this on Gemma 44 (Section 4, App. A.6). ∎

The fourth result sharpens the LN-kernel test from a binary check on direction alignment into a quantitative diagnostic. Proposition 2 predicts that the bottom singular direction u⊥u_{\bot} of the post-final-norm centred covariance equals γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|. What this leaves out is how deeply the kernel has formed: at random initialisation the predicted direction is the kernel by construction, but on a trained network the actual smallest eigenvalue can be orders of magnitude smaller along some other direction that training has driven toward zero. The Schur ratio captures this depth.

Lemma 5 (Schur-ratio prefactor).

For a LayerNorm-fed Linear layer with Gaussian-isotropic input at the post-final-norm position, the per-block Schur ratio R⁡(h):=λmin​(Aℓ)/(Aℓ)u,uR(h):=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})\,/\,(A_{\ell})_{u,u} along the predicted direction u=γ−1/‖γ−1‖u=\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| converges to 11 at the asymptotic limit. Equivalently, the dead-channel depth Δγ:=1−R⁡(h)∈[0,1]\Delta_{\gamma}:=1-R(h)\in[0,1] tracks the finite-NN Marchenko–Pastur dispersion ∼2​h/N−h/N\sim 2\sqrt{h/N}-h/N at random initialisation, and saturates at ≈1\approx 1 when training opens additional dead directions strictly deeper than uu.

Sketch.

Under Gaussian-isotropic post-LN input, the activation Gram Aℓ=𝔼⁡[X​X⊤]A_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[XX^{\top}] at the dead row uu has the closed-form structure α​I+β​𝟏𝟏⊤\alpha I+\beta\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} on the orthogonal complement of uu. The Schur complement at the dead row gives a rank-11 outer-product cancellation c=(h−1)/(π⁡(π+h−2))≤1/πc=(h-1)/(\pi(\pi+h-2))\leq 1/\pi, leaving R⁡(h)=1−c≥1−1/πR(h)=1-c\geq 1-1/\pi at finite hh and R⁡(h)→1R(h)\to 1 as h→∞h\to\infty. The Marchenko–Pastur term is the bottom-edge dispersion of the sample-covariance estimator at finite NN. ∎

The four results compose into a single empirical pipeline. Proposition 2 gives the LN architectural baseline, validated at four-decimal precision on 99 LN models. Proposition 3 is the dichotomy’s negative, validated on 55 RMSNorm models. Corollary 4 is the residual-DAG consequence, tested on all 1414 models in our set. Lemma 5 converts the LN-kernel test into a per-checkpoint accumulation budget on the Pythia size sweep. Section 4 carries each test in turn.

4 Experiments

We test the four predictions of §3 on a cross-architecture set of 1414 pretrained transformers (160160M–3535B parameters; objectives span next-token CE, supervised image classification, image SSL, image–text contrastive, and video SSL). Each prediction targets a different aspect of the dead-direction structure. Corollary 4 stakes a residual-DAG architectural claim that should hold across all 1414 models irrespective of normalisation: the smallest residual-stream singular value cannot decrease block-to-block under the no-cancellation hypothesis. Propositions 2 and 3 together stake an architectural dichotomy: LN admits a parameter-readable kernel direction γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|, RMSNorm does not. Lemma 5 sharpens the LN-kernel test from a binary check on the measured bottom direction u⊥u_{\bot} to a quantitative per-checkpoint diagnostic via the Schur ratio Δγ:=1−R⁡(h)\Delta_{\gamma}:=1-R(h). Each test runs at the cost of a single forward pass per checkpoint with no SGLD chain and no gradient access; we validate each in turn below.

(a) Pipeline and protocol.

The pipeline captures residual-stream activations Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} per block, accumulates a chunked covariance (fp3232 default; fp6464 recommended for inputs with σmax≳105\sigma_{\max}\gtrsim 10^{5} to anchor the bottom of the spectrum), then fp6464-eigendecomposes once per layer to recover σmin\sigma_{\min}, σmax\sigma_{\max}, top/bottom singular directions, and Shannon-entropy effective rank (Roy and Vetterli, 2007; Sanyal et al., 2020). Per-checkpoint σmin\sigma_{\min} alone is real-time-cheap on a single RTX 3090 (≤2\leq 2 s through Qwen3.6-27B at fp3232 cov, ∼3{\sim}3–5×5\times slower at fp6464); the full residual-stream fingerprint takes <2<2 s at Pythia-1B, 88 s at Qwen3.5-4B, 160160 s at Qwen3.6-27B at fp3232 cov (Appendix A.5). All three predictions are read from a single forward pass per checkpoint, with no SGLD chain and no gradient access. Calibration corpus: WikiText-103 validation for language models, ImageNet validation for vision transformers; observable values are input-distribution-invariant under the centred-covariance protocol, confirmed empirically across 55 standard ViTs at |Δ​cos|<10−6|\Delta\cos|<10^{-6} between synthetic-noise and real-image calibration.

(b) σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance.

Corollary 4 (§3) holds on 12/1412/14 pretrained transformers under the uniform text-only protocol (fp6464 centred-cov, against the true input embedding X0X_{0}). The two failures are both Gemma 44 releases: Gemma4-31B (non-monotone depth-decreasing, a finite ∼18×\sim\!18\times net σmin\sigma_{\min} reduction at the output) and Gemma4-E4B (an intermediate dip that recovers). A family discriminator across Gemma 11–44 localises the failure to the Gemma 44 release: pre-LN Gemma-11 and Peri-LN Gemma-22/33 all preserve σmin\sigma_{\min}, and only Gemma 44 (also Peri-LN) fails, so the failure does not track the normalisation placement. A five-mechanism ablation rules out four further candidate causes and localises the collapse to the MLP sub-layer; the residual cause is a calibration-distribution effect of Gemma 44’s encoder-free native multimodality (App. A.6). Text-only calibration leaves the vision and audio soft-token subspaces dormant: under the full input distribution the dip dissolves on the tri-modal Gemma4-E4B (a distribution-relative dead direction), while a residual intrinsic near-dead direction persists, above the fp3232 measurement floor, on the bi-modal Gemma4-31B. So 13/1413/14 hold once each model is calibrated on its own input distribution. The prediction also holds dynamically: on 88 Pythia-1B pretraining revisions (step1 to step143000), the ratio ≥1\geq 1 at every depth on every revision (Fig. 2b), amplitude rising from ∼12×\sim 12\times to a peak of ∼299×\sim 299\times before settling to ∼206×\sim 206\times at the mature checkpoint. Proposition 2’s cosine stays ≥0.998\geq 0.998 across all 88 revisions while the uniform-γ\gamma approximation decays as γ\gamma disperses (Fig. 2d): the prediction’s γ\gamma-dependence is what tracks the dispersion. σmin\sigma_{\min} profiling at fp6464 cov is the cheapest signal we know that surfaces this kind of residual-branch pathology in pretrained transformers.

(c) Norm-side algebraic dichotomy.

For each of the 99 LN-equipped pretrained transformers we read γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| off the terminal-norm affine and compare it to the bottom singular direction u⊥u_{\bot} of the post-final-norm centred covariance, computed via fp6464 SVD on a calibration batch. Proposition 2 predicts the two should agree exactly. Empirically |cos⁡(u⊥,γ−1/‖γ−1‖)|≥0.9999|\cos(u_{\bot},\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|)|\geq 0.9999 on 9/99/9 models, mean 0.999990.99999. Four-decimal alignment is the load-bearing test: the random-direction baseline at typical residual widths is |cos|≈1/d≤0.05|\cos|\approx 1/\sqrt{d}\leq 0.05, so the empirical match sits ×±×37\!\times\pm 9\!\times above the null and would be unreachable by any non-architectural mechanism. The complementary RMSNorm test evaluates Proposition 3: across 55 RMSNorm models and n=718n{=}718 (model, position) cells, |cos⁡(u⊥,earg⁡min⁡γ)||\cos(u_{\bot},e_{\arg\min\gamma})| has mean 0.0150.015, indistinguishable from the random null. The two readings together classify any pretrained transformer’s normalisation choice from a closed-form inspection of its forward-map projector, before any forward pass on the checkpoint.

(d) Schur-ratio diagnostic: algebraic null vs trained singular structure.

The Schur-ratio prefactor (Lem. 5) yields a width-only invariant R⁡(h):=λmin​(Aℓ)/(Aℓ)u,uR(h):=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})/(A_{\ell})_{u,u} along the predicted direction u=γ−1/‖γ−1‖u=\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|, evaluated at the QKV input of every attention block (a Type-A site: a Linear layer fed by a LayerNorm). We sweep 1111 pretrained transformers (55 LayerNorm Pythia sizes plus 66 RMSNorm models) at N=131,072N=131{,}072 tokens fp6464 covariance, each model measured at the trained checkpoint and at random init across 55 initialization seeds (Tab. 1). At random init on Pythia 160160M–2.82.8B, the pooled-median Δγ​(h):=1−R⁡(h)\Delta_{\gamma}(h):=1-R(h) across 55 seeds and all attention sites holds within ±0.03\pm 0.03 of zero, consistent with the prediction’s algebraic limit R→1R\to 1 up to fp6464 covariance noise; Pythia-7070M (h=512h{=}512, 66 blocks) reads pooled-median Δγ≈0.23\Delta_{\gamma}\approx 0.23, the small-block, wider-eigengap edge of the sweep. On the trained checkpoint Δγ→1\Delta_{\gamma}\to 1 uniformly across all 55 Pythia sizes, indicating that training opens dead directions ∼103×\sim\!10^{3}\times deeper along some other coordinate (Pythia-7070M block 00: λmin​(A)=1.96⋅10−3\lambda_{\min}(A)=1.96\cdot 10^{-3} vs (A)γ−1,γ−1=2.40(A)_{\gamma^{-1},\gamma^{-1}}=2.40; ratio 1.2⋅1031.2\cdot 10^{3}). RMSNorm models start at Δγ∈[0.80,0.97]\Delta_{\gamma}\in[0.80,0.97] at random init (no universal kernel exists, so the algebraic baseline is absent) and saturate at ≈1\approx 1 once trained; Lemma 5’s asymptotic limit holds for LN-fed Type-A sites and not for RMSNorm-fed ones, as predicted. Full per-row analysis, including the cross-model figure (Fig. 6), the Pythia width sweep, and the noise-floor recovery protocol for blocks where both λmin​(A)\lambda_{\min}(A) and (A)u,u(A)_{u,u} sit at the fp6464 cov floor, is in App. A.6.

5 Discussion

What we showed.

The framework’s central architecture-side prediction (γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| as the post-final-LN dead direction, readable from the affine parameter alone) holds at four-decimal precision on every LayerNorm pretrained transformer in our set (9/99/9 centered) and is correctly absent on RMSNorm models (5/55/5, |cos|≤0.10|\cos|\leq 0.10 centered). The same algebraic null acts as a per-checkpoint reference: on the trained checkpoint, the Schur ratio Δγ\Delta_{\gamma} along the predicted direction collapses from the finite-NN Marchenko–Pastur drift on the smallest cell (≈0.37\approx 0.37 at h=512h{=}512, within ±0.06\pm 0.06 of zero at h≥768h\geq 768 on the Pythia sweep) to ≈1\approx 1 across all sizes on the trained checkpoint, so training has opened additional dead directions ∼103×\sim\!10^{3}\times deeper along the same coordinate. The gap between random-init and trained Δγ\Delta_{\gamma} is itself a forward-pass-only diagnostic of accumulated singular structure that no prior method extracts. Two consequences follow without further machinery: residual-stream σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance on 13/1413/14 pretrained transformers once each model is read on its own input distribution (both Gemma 44 releases dip under the uniform text-only protocol; multimodal recalibration dissolves Gemma4-E4B’s dip as a dormant-modality artifact and leaves Gemma4-31B as the one genuine intrinsic dead direction the same read pinpoints), and an algebraic LN/RMSNorm dichotomy that classifies any pretrained transformer’s normalisation choice from a single closed-form test on γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|. The fingerprint reads only the activation covariance and the LN affine, so the estimator question that scopes the trajectory rate-fit does not reach it: σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance is a singular-value of the forward-pass covariance with no loss gradient and no Fisher estimator involved, and γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| is read from the affine parameter alone (Remark 4). The residual prefactor that distinguishes the stored loss-gradient covariance from the population Fisher on a learned trajectory enters neither.

Alternative explanations considered.

(i) Projector-kernel coincidence. If γ\gamma were uniform, γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| would collapse to 𝟏d/d\mathbf{1}_{d}/\sqrt{d} (LN’s mean-subtraction projector kernel) and the prediction would be indistinguishable from the trivial null. Three of the nine LN models break that regime materially: DINOv22-base has |cos⁡(γ−1/‖γ−1‖,𝟏d/d)|=0.56|\cos(\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|,\mathbf{1}_{d}/\sqrt{d})|=0.56 from the affine, DINOv33-ViT-L has 0.0450.045, and ViT-B/16 has 0.0070.007 (the most extreme, its γ\gamma nearly orthogonal to 𝟏d\mathbf{1}_{d}). On all three, the measured u⊥u_{\bot} tracks the exact γ−1\gamma^{-1} prediction to ≥3\geq 3 decimals while the uniform-γ\gamma approximation tracks the smaller cosine the affine actually predicts; the γ\gamma-dependence carries the prediction. (ii) fp3232 tautology. At fp3232 cov, several models read σmin​(X0)=0\sigma_{\min}(X_{0})=0 from the accumulator floor; only fp6464 resolves the actual values, and only then is the strict ratio test passable or failable. For the two massive-activation RMSNorm models the binding floor is the bf1616 forward capture as well as the fp3232 covariance: fp3232 forward and fp6464 cov are both required to resolve them. The Gemma 44 failures persist at fp6464.

Limitations.

Two are load-bearing. (a) The origin of Gemma4-31B’s intrinsic dead direction is open. The σmin\sigma_{\min} collapse is dissociated from five candidate mechanisms (γ\gamma-kernel formation, residual-vs-delta alignment, the Peri-LN sandwich-norm pattern, sink-token estimator bias, post-pretraining stage), localised to the MLP sub-layer, and on the tri-modal Gemma4-E4B traced to a calibration-distribution effect: the text-only dip is a dormant-modality artifact that dissolves under the model’s full text++image++audio distribution. On the bi-modal Gemma4-31B a genuine intrinsic near-dead direction persists above the fp3232 measurement floor under image calibration; the training-recipe difference from the earlier Gemma releases that would explain why this checkpoint carries one remains untested. (b) Architecture coverage is LN-vs-RMSNorm only. BatchNorm (CNN backbones), GroupNorm (diffusion U-Nets), and DyT are structurally different and remain open empirical cells; the algebraic test extends to them by inspection (Proposition 2’s mean-subtraction projector is the structural property that determines whether a γ\gamma-derived universal kernel direction exists), but per-norm validation on real architectures is left to future work.

Falsifier.

The central prediction has a single clean falsifier: an LN-equipped pretrained transformer for which |cos⁡(u⊥,γ−1/‖γ−1‖)||\cos(u_{\bot},\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|)| at the post-final-norm position is bounded away from 11 on the trained checkpoint at fp6464 centered cov. Across the 1414-model set we did not find one; any such counter-example would force a structural revision of Proposition 2.

Implications: architectural vs training-induced singular structure.

The split between random-init and trained Δγ\Delta_{\gamma} operationalises a worldview about how singular structure accumulates in transformers. Every LN block carries one architecturally guaranteed dead direction, γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|, present at random init and predictable from the affine alone. Training opens deeper kernels along the same coordinate, and the gap between architectural baseline and trained depth is the training-induced component. RMSNorm models have no architectural component; their dead structure is entirely training-induced, and their σmin\sigma_{\min} depth-invariance pass rate is comparable to LN’s at convergence. The LN/RMSNorm trade is therefore between capacity (RMSNorm preserves all dd residual-stream coordinates) and structural predictability (LN gives a closed-form, parameter-readable anchor). Modern LLMs weighted capacity above predictability when they switched to RMSNorm. The predictability remains valuable wherever LN is still in use, both for diagnostics on existing checkpoints and for analysis of pretrained vision transformers.

Practitioner takeaways.

Four concrete actions become available. (1) Free architectural reference and protocol sanity check. On any LN-equipped checkpoint, γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| is the bottom singular direction of the post-final-norm centred covariance at random init by algebraic identity, with no compute required. The same direction doubles as a measurement-protocol check: if the empirical u⊥u_{\bot} on a calibration batch does not match γ−1/‖γ−1‖\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\| within fp6464 precision, the protocol is wrong (incorrect hook, raw-Gram instead of centred-cov, fp3232 accumulator floor). (2) Importance-based LoRA placement. For methods that select adapter directions by importance score (AdaLoRA, gradient-importance LoRA), γ−1\gamma^{-1} at LN block boundaries should be excluded from the candidate set. Rank put there cannot adapt to input variation because the LN output has zero variance along γ−1\gamma^{-1}; it can only learn a bias term. Random-initialised LoRA overlaps γ−1\gamma^{-1} at the 1/d1/\sqrt{d} level and is mostly unaffected, but importance-based methods that align with high-variance directions can waste rank if they fail to exclude this one. (3) Investigation signal on residual-branch pathologies. An fp6464-cov σmin\sigma_{\min} pass surfaces architectural anomalies (the Gemma 44 MLP-localised collapse) that standard fp3232-cov pipelines miss because the noise floor σmax⋅εfp32\sigma_{\max}\cdot\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fp32}}} sits above the active spectrum. The diagnostic flags an anomaly worth investigating, not a verdict on functional pathology; without matched-recipe controls we cannot tell whether the anomaly is a defect or a deliberate trade. The value is targeting expensive downstream investigation rather than running it blind. (4) Norm-architecture screening for designers and compression researchers. The algebraic dichotomy classifies any normalisation scheme by inspection of its forward-map projector, without retraining. For architecture designers introducing new schemes (DyT, ScaleNorm, FixUp, sandwich-norm variants), it predicts whether the scheme carries a γ\gamma-derived universal kernel before any empirical study. For compression researchers, it predicts which models admit SliceGPT-style affine-folding into adjacent weights.

Future work.

Continual-learning safe-direction constraints: orthogonal-gradient and null-space methods identify these directions empirically; the LN-kernel proposition gives an analytic, pretrained-model-readable instance. Rank-collapse early warning during pretraining: the static observables are computable per checkpoint with no gradient access, natural candidates for periodic monitoring at scale (Fig. 2 is the existence proof). Norm-cell extensions: BatchNorm, GroupNorm, and DyT are forward-pass-cheap tests that extend the dichotomy beyond LN/RMSNorm.
